title: Ang 370–411: Guru Arjan in Asa
hookLine: a great run of hymns, including your will is sweet on ang 394
tomorrow: why is a hymn about war so full of brides?

lines: THREE DAYS OUT. NO TENT. RAIN.
cards: Three days to the wedding. The tent company calls: the rental fell through. The forecast says rain.
An aunt is on speaker, her voice climbing, and everyone turns to the bride to see whether she'll cry. She doesn't. She says, quietly, a line her grandmother says: tera keeaa meethaa laagai.
What You do tastes sweet to me. It sounds like giving up. It isn't.

teach.b: Guru Arjan's Asa hymns run from ang 370 to 411, a long stretch, and in the middle sits this couplet, in paraphrase: what You do tastes sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Two lines.
Notice what they don't say. They don't say the rain is good, or that the tent doesn't matter.

teach.h: ASK FOR ONE THING: THE NAME.
teach.b: They say the doing of the One tastes sweet, and then they ask for one thing. Not a better forecast. The Name.

teach.h: SWEET, NOT JUST PUT UP WITH.
teach.b: And sweet is a strange word for it. You'd expect accept, or put up with. Sweet is what you say about food you'd reach for again.
Guru Arjan isn't describing gritted teeth.
He's describing a taste that has changed.
Tradition holds that he lived this line in his own last days, the hardest of his life, and Sikhs remember him that way, gently. It isn't a switch you flip on a bad Thursday.
It's a taste you grow into, by asking for the Name over and over, the way the couplet does, until the plan falling apart and the sweetness can sit at the same table.

how: Guru Arjan's Asa hymns, headed Mahala 5, are read in order and sung as kirtan; the couplet on ang 394 is one Sikhs often turn to in hard times, remembering the fifth Guru.

the page where Guru Arjan's Asa hymns begin

s: the ang 394 couplet says bad things are secretly good
it says what the One does tastes sweet, and asks for the Name; it never calls the rain good.
the couplet asks for only one thing
Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name.
'sweet will' means pretending you aren't upset
sweet is a taste that changes over time, not a mask over the hurt.

games.q: your sister doesn't get into the school she wanted. through tears she says 'it's fine.' what fits ang 394?
o: let her be sad, and stay close; the sweetness comes slowly, with the Name.
tell her to stop crying: the will is sweet, so she shouldn't be upset.
agree it's all unfair and help her stay angry about it.
games.why: the couplet isn't a rule against tears. it's a taste you grow into by asking for the Name, over and over.

practice: Read ang 394 if you can, and find the couplet. Say it aloud once, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in English: what You do tastes sweet to me.
Then sit with one thing this week that didn't go your way, and let the words rest beside it, without forcing anything.

wordCard.voice: Ang 370. The page where Guru Arjan's long run of Asa hymns begins; the sweet will couplet waits on ang 394.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: meetha, sweet, in tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do tastes sweet.

carryVoice: Hold onto: sweet will, a taste you grow into, one ask for the Name at a time. Talk soon.
